lessons.title: What is System Design?
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A feature can work correctly on one laptop and still fail in production when traffic grows, dependencies slow down, data becomes large, or a region becomes unavailable. System design is the discipline of choosing boundaries, data flows, and failure behavior before those pressures become emergencies.

## How it works

Start with requirements, then draw the request path: client, edge, application services, data stores, asynchronous workers, and observability. For each hop, identify ownership, expected load, latency budget, data durability, and what happens when the hop is unavailable. The architecture is not a collection of fashionable boxes; it is a set of justified trade-offs.

## Design decisions

- Separate functional requirements from quality attributes such as latency, availability, durability, and cost.
- Estimate order of magnitude before choosing technology.
- Design degraded modes so the system has a useful response when a dependency fails.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is designing only the happy path: one server, one database, and no timeout, retry, or recovery plan. The system looks simple until the first traffic spike or dependency outage.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** Designing a city before building houses: roads, utilities, zoning, and emergency routes matter because individual buildings interact.

**Real-system connection:** A streaming application separates playback APIs, recommendation systems, storage, and edge delivery because each path has different load and failure characteristics.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **system design**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design a photo-sharing application for 1 million daily active users and identify the first bottleneck.
keyPoints: System design turns requirements into explicit technical trade-offs.
Failure handling and observability belong in the initial design.

lessons.title: Client-Server Architecture
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Applications need a clean contract between the software used by a person or device and the systems that store data and perform shared work. Without this separation, every client would need direct knowledge of databases, secrets, and internal topology.

## How it works

A client sends requests over a network protocol such as HTTPS. A server authenticates the caller, validates input, performs business logic, reads or writes data, and returns a response. The server may itself call other services. Stateless application servers are easier to scale because any healthy instance can handle the next request; durable session state belongs in a shared store or signed client token when appropriate.

## Design decisions

- Choose request-response for immediate answers and asynchronous workflows for long-running work.
- Version contracts so old mobile clients do not break when the server evolves.
- Keep trust boundaries clear: never trust validation performed only in the browser.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is storing important session state only in one server process. A load balancer sends the next request to a different instance and the user appears logged out or loses in-progress work.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A restaurant: customers place orders through a waiter instead of entering the kitchen. The kitchen can reorganize internally while the menu remains a stable contract.

**Real-system connection:** A mobile banking client uses HTTPS APIs, but balance checks, authorization, audit logging, and transfers execute on controlled servers.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **client-server architecture**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Explain how a shopping cart behaves across two API server instances.
keyPoints: Clients consume contracts; servers protect data and enforce rules.
Network calls fail and need timeouts, idempotency, and compatibility planning.

lessons.title: Databases: SQL vs NoSQL
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Applications need durable storage, but different data models optimize different questions. Choosing a database by popularity creates expensive migrations later. The correct starting point is access patterns, consistency requirements, write volume, query flexibility, and operational skills.

## How it works

Relational databases store tables with constraints and transactions. They are strong defaults for orders, payments, accounts, and workflows where relationships and correctness matter. NoSQL is an umbrella term: document databases model aggregates, key-value stores optimize direct lookups, and wide-column databases support large partitioned write workloads. Many mature systems use more than one store while keeping a clear source of truth.

## Design decisions

- Prefer a relational database until a measured workload or data model justifies another choice.
- Model keys around the queries the application actually performs.
- Separate operational storage from search indexes, caches, and analytical warehouses.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is adding a document database to avoid schema design, then discovering inconsistent fields, missing indexes, and difficult reporting. Flexible schema still requires governance.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A library: a relational catalog is ideal for precise records and relationships, while a fast lookup counter or full-text search index solves different retrieval problems.

**Real-system connection:** An e-commerce platform can keep orders in PostgreSQL, cache hot products in Redis, index product text in Elasticsearch, and store product images in object storage.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **database selection**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Choose storage components for an online marketplace and justify each one.
keyPoints: Database choice follows access patterns and correctness needs.
SQL and NoSQL stores solve different problems rather than forming a simple ranking.
Polyglot persistence needs explicit ownership and synchronization.

lessons.title: Caching Fundamentals
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Repeatedly computing or fetching the same result wastes time and capacity. A cache stores reusable data closer to the request path so the system responds faster and protects expensive dependencies. The difficult part is not adding a cache; it is defining freshness and failure behavior.

## How it works

In cache-aside, the application checks the cache, reads the database on a miss, and stores the result with a TTL. Cache keys must include every dimension that changes the response, such as user, locale, or authorization scope. TTL jitter, request coalescing, and stale-while-revalidate behavior can prevent many clients from rebuilding the same value simultaneously.

## Design decisions

- Cache only data with meaningful reuse.
- Define invalidation or acceptable staleness before implementation.
- Treat the database or durable store as the source of truth unless explicitly designing otherwise.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is a popular key expiring at once. Thousands of requests miss, hit the database simultaneously, and create a cache stampede that takes down the source system.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A receptionist keeps frequently requested forms at the front desk rather than walking to the archive for every visitor.

**Real-system connection:** A product catalog caches popular product details for seconds or minutes while inventory confirmation still checks an authoritative transactional store.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **caching**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design a cache for a product page viewed heavily during a flash sale.
keyPoints: Caches trade freshness for speed and reduced load.
Key design and TTL policy determine correctness.
Stampede protection and monitoring are required for hot data.
lessons.analogy: A receptionist keeps frequently requested forms at the front desk rather than walking to the archive for every visitor.
lessons.example: A product catalog caches popular product details for seconds or minutes while inventory confirmation still checks an authoritative transactional store.

lessons.title: Load Balancing
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

One server eventually reaches a capacity limit or becomes unavailable. Load balancing spreads traffic across healthy instances so capacity can grow horizontally and a single application-server failure does not take down the service.

## How it works

Layer 4 load balancers route connections using transport details such as IP and port. Layer 7 balancers understand HTTP and can route by host, path, header, or cookie. Health checks remove unhealthy instances, while connection draining lets in-flight work finish during deployment. Algorithms include round-robin, least connections, weighted routing, and consistent-hash-based approaches for selected stateful workloads.

## Design decisions

- Use readiness checks that reflect whether an instance can serve real traffic.
- Keep application servers stateless or deliberately externalize state.
- Align timeouts from client through proxy to backend.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is using a shallow health check that always returns success while the application cannot reach its database. The load balancer continues sending real requests to a broken instance.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A supermarket opens additional checkout lanes and directs customers to available cashiers instead of letting one queue grow indefinitely.

**Real-system connection:** A web platform puts multiple API instances behind a managed Layer 7 load balancer and drains old instances during rolling deployments.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **load balancing**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Explain why adding ten API servers may not fix a slow checkout endpoint.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Adding instances improves capacity until a shared dependency becomes the bottleneck.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use meaningful readiness probes, shared state stores, timeout budgets, and database capacity monitoring.
keyPoints: Load balancers improve availability and horizontal scale.
Health checks and draining are operationally critical.
They do not remove downstream bottlenecks such as a saturated database.
lessons.analogy: A supermarket opens additional checkout lanes and directs customers to available cashiers instead of letting one queue grow indefinitely.
lessons.example: A web platform puts multiple API instances behind a managed Layer 7 load balancer and drains old instances during rolling deployments.

lessons.title: Message Queues
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Some work should not execute inside the user-facing request. Sending email, generating thumbnails, processing invoices, and calling slow integrations can delay responses and fail unpredictably. A queue decouples acceptance of work from execution.

## How it works

A producer writes a message to a broker. One or more consumers retrieve messages, process them, and acknowledge success. Failed messages may be retried with delay and eventually moved to a dead-letter queue for investigation. Delivery is commonly at least once, so consumers need idempotency. Queue depth and oldest-message age expose whether consumers are keeping up.

## Design decisions

- Use queues to absorb bursts and isolate slow downstream work.
- Design message payloads as stable contracts with identifiers rather than giant mutable snapshots.
- Set retry limits, backoff, and dead-letter handling.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is retrying a poison message forever. One malformed event repeatedly crashes consumers, consumes capacity, and prevents healthy work from progressing.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A parcel sorting center: accepting a package and recording it is separate from the later steps that route and deliver it.

**Real-system connection:** An image-upload API stores metadata, enqueues a thumbnail job, and returns promptly. Workers scale independently and update processing status later.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **message queues**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design an email-sending worker that avoids duplicate emails after retries.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Asynchrony improves resilience but introduces eventual consistency and operational visibility needs.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Monitor queue depth and age, use idempotency keys, and quarantine poison messages.
keyPoints: Queues improve decoupling and burst tolerance.
Backpressure, retry policy, and DLQs are core design elements.
lessons.analogy: A parcel sorting center: accepting a package and recording it is separate from the later steps that route and deliver it.
lessons.example: An image-upload API stores metadata, enqueues a thumbnail job, and returns promptly. Workers scale independently and update processing status later.

lessons.title: CDNs and a Complete Web Architecture
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A production web system is a path, not a single server. Users may be far from the origin, static files can dominate bandwidth, and different requests need different treatment. A complete architecture combines edge delivery, traffic control, application compute, durable storage, caching, background processing, and observability.

## How it works

A typical request reaches DNS, then a CDN or edge layer, a WAF, a load balancer or gateway, and stateless application servers. Cacheable assets are served near the user. Dynamic API calls reach services that use a transactional database, cache, object storage, and queues. Logs, metrics, and traces describe system health. Multi-zone deployment and backups reduce common failure risks.

## Design decisions

- Separate static delivery from dynamic APIs.
- Use object storage and a CDN for large immutable files.
- Design the architecture around critical journeys, not around drawing every possible component.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is adding many components without defining ownership or fallback behavior. Complexity then creates more failure modes than value.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** An airport: signs and routing direct passengers, security filters entry, gates serve destinations, baggage moves asynchronously, and operations monitor the whole flow.

**Real-system connection:** A photo-sharing product stores images in object storage, serves them through a CDN, routes APIs through a load balancer, caches profile reads, and processes thumbnails with workers.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **complete web architecture**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Draw the minimum production architecture for a global photo-sharing application.
keyPoints: Edge caching reduces latency and origin load.
A complete diagram should include data, asynchronous work, security, and observability.
Every component requires a reason and a failure plan.

lessons.example: A photo-sharing product stores images in object storage, serves them through a CDN, routes APIs through a load balancer, caches profile reads, and processes thumbnails with workers.

lessons.title: REST, GraphQL, and gRPC
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Services need contracts that clients can understand and evolve against. REST, GraphQL, and gRPC are tools with different strengths; choosing one universally creates unnecessary complexity.

## How it works

REST exposes resources over HTTP and works well for public APIs, caching, and broad tooling. GraphQL lets a client request a shaped response through a schema, useful when frontends need flexible aggregation but requiring query-cost controls. gRPC uses strongly typed contracts and efficient binary transport, often suitable for internal service-to-service communication and streaming.

## Design decisions

- Choose based on consumers, network boundaries, evolution needs, and observability.
- Apply pagination, timeouts, validation, and versioning regardless of protocol.
- Prevent GraphQL queries or gRPC fan-out from hiding expensive backend work.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is exposing an unrestricted GraphQL endpoint where one deeply nested query triggers hundreds of downstream calls and overloads the system.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** Transport choices are like shipping methods: envelopes, custom packing lists, and freight containers each fit different cargo and destinations.

**Real-system connection:** A public developer API may use REST, a mobile aggregation layer may use GraphQL, and internal low-latency services may use gRPC.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **API style selection**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Choose APIs for a marketplace with mobile apps, partner integrations, and internal services.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Flexibility and efficiency increase the need for schema governance, tooling, and cost controls.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Add request limits, schema review, observability, pagination, and compatibility tests.
keyPoints: Strong contracts and backward compatibility matter more than trend selection.
Hidden backend cost must be bounded.
lessons.analogy: Transport choices are like shipping methods: envelopes, custom packing lists, and freight containers each fit different cargo and destinations.
lessons.example: A public developer API may use REST, a mobile aggregation layer may use GraphQL, and internal low-latency services may use gRPC.

lessons.title: Database Indexing
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A database can store millions of rows correctly and still become slow if each query scans far more data than necessary. Indexes create additional structures that help the database locate matching rows efficiently.

## How it works

A B-tree index is useful for equality and range conditions; composite index order matters because the leading columns shape efficient lookups. Full-text, hash, spatial, and specialized indexes solve different access patterns. Every index consumes storage and adds write work, so the goal is not to index everything. Query plans reveal whether the database scans, seeks, sorts, or joins efficiently.

## Design decisions

- Design indexes from real query patterns.
- Use execution plans and production-like data volumes.
- Remove redundant indexes and monitor write amplification.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is indexing each column independently while the real query filters by tenant and status then sorts by created time. The database still performs expensive work because the index does not match the access pattern.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A book index helps find a topic without reading every page, but adding an index entry for every possible phrase would make the book unwieldy.

**Real-system connection:** An orders API may need a composite index on tenant_id, status, and created_at to list recent pending orders efficiently.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **database indexing**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Optimize a query listing recent unpaid invoices for one customer.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **More indexes speed selected reads while slowing writes and migrations.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Inspect query plans, measure slow queries, and align composite indexes with access patterns.
keyPoints: Indexes accelerate reads by spending storage and write cost.
lessons.analogy: A book index helps find a topic without reading every page, but adding an index entry for every possible phrase would make the book unwieldy.
lessons.example: An orders API may need a composite index on tenant_id, status, and created_at to list recent pending orders efficiently.

lessons.title: Database Sharding
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A single database primary has practical limits for storage, write throughput, and maintenance windows. Sharding splits data into independent partitions so the workload can grow beyond one node.

## How it works

A router maps each request to a shard using a shard key such as tenant, user, region, or a hashed identifier. Range sharding simplifies locality but can create hot ranges. Hash sharding distributes load but makes range queries harder. Virtual shards or buckets reduce migration risk because logical partitions can move between physical nodes.

## Design decisions

- Choose a key that distributes traffic and supports common queries.
- Plan rebalancing before the first production shard split.
- Avoid cross-shard joins and distributed transactions on critical paths.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is sharding an orders table by creation date. Today's shard receives almost every new write while older shards remain idle.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A growing city divides services into districts, but the district boundaries must match where people live and travel.

**Real-system connection:** A multi-tenant SaaS product can route tenants to virtual shards, then move selected tenant buckets as workload grows.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **database sharding**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Choose a shard key for a multi-tenant accounting platform.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Horizontal capacity improves, while operations, migrations, and global queries become harder.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Introduce logical buckets, routing metadata, hot-shard metrics, and tested migration tooling.
lessons.analogy: A growing city divides services into districts, but the district boundaries must match where people live and travel.
lessons.example: A multi-tenant SaaS product can route tenants to virtual shards, then move selected tenant buckets as workload grows.

lessons.title: Connection Pooling
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Database and network connections are not free. Creating a new connection for every request adds handshake latency and can overwhelm a database that supports far fewer concurrent sessions than application requests.

## How it works

A connection pool keeps a bounded set of reusable connections. Requests borrow a connection briefly and return it immediately after the transaction. Pool size should reflect database capacity, application replica count, query duration, and workload concurrency. A proxy pooler can help when many application instances or serverless functions connect to one database.

## Design decisions

- Bound pool size across the whole fleet, not only per instance.
- Keep transactions short.
- Monitor wait time, active connections, and database saturation together.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is scaling application Pods from 10 to 100 while each Pod opens 50 database connections. The database receives thousands of sessions and fails during the traffic spike.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A hotel has a limited set of rooms; a booking desk reuses them efficiently rather than constructing a new room for each guest.

**Real-system connection:** A PostgreSQL-backed API uses a bounded pool per process and a database-aware proxy when bursty workers would otherwise open too many connections.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **connection pooling**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Calculate a safe per-Pod pool size when 40 Pods share a 400-connection database budget.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **A larger pool can raise concurrency but may reduce database throughput through contention.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Set bounded pools, instrument wait time, and apply backpressure before the database collapses.
keyPoints: Pools reduce handshake overhead and protect dependencies.
lessons.analogy: A hotel has a limited set of rooms; a booking desk reuses them efficiently rather than constructing a new room for each guest.
lessons.example: A PostgreSQL-backed API uses a bounded pool per process and a database-aware proxy when bursty workers would otherwise open too many connections.

lessons.title: Rate Limiting
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A service must protect itself from abusive clients, accidental loops, and sudden bursts. Rate limiting provides fairness and preserves capacity before overload spreads to slower dependencies.

## How it works

A token bucket accumulates tokens at a steady rate and allows bounded bursts. A sliding window estimates usage more smoothly than a fixed window. Limits may apply by IP, user, API key, tenant, endpoint, or cost unit. Distributed implementations often use an edge gateway or a fast shared store, with an explicit fail-open or fail-closed policy.

## Design decisions

- Protect expensive endpoints differently from cheap ones.
- Return a clear 429 response and retry guidance.
- Combine rate limits with quotas, concurrency limits, and DDoS controls.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is applying only one global limit. A single noisy tenant consumes the budget and blocks healthy customers.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A venue controls entry with tickets per minute and a limited waiting area so the building remains safe.

**Real-system connection:** An AI API can charge requests by token budget rather than counting a cheap metadata call and an expensive generation call equally.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **rate limiting**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design limits for a file-conversion API with free and paid plans.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Stricter limits protect capacity but can reject valid burst traffic.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use token buckets, tenant-aware keys, concurrency caps, metrics, and retry headers.
keyPoints: Rate limiting preserves fairness and capacity.
lessons.analogy: A venue controls entry with tickets per minute and a limited waiting area so the building remains safe.
lessons.example: An AI API can charge requests by token budget rather than counting a cheap metadata call and an expensive generation call equally.

lessons.title: Authentication and Authorization
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A secure backend must answer two separate questions: who is calling, and what is that caller allowed to do. Mixing them creates authorization gaps that are difficult to detect in testing.

## How it works

Authentication establishes identity using sessions, tokens, certificates, or delegated identity protocols. Authorization evaluates permissions for the requested action and resource. Short-lived access tokens, refresh-token protection, server-side revocation strategy, least privilege, and audit logs are practical controls. Authorization must be enforced on the server for every sensitive operation.

## Design decisions

- Keep identity verification separate from resource-level permission checks.
- Validate token issuer, audience, signature, expiry, and intended use.
- Prefer centralized policy guidance with enforcement close to the resource.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is checking that a user is logged in but not checking whether the requested invoice belongs to that user's tenant. The result is an insecure direct object reference.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** An office badge proves identity at the entrance, but room access still depends on the employee's role and the room's policy.

**Real-system connection:** A SaaS backend verifies an OAuth access token, resolves tenant membership, applies role and resource policy, and records sensitive changes in an audit log.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **authentication and authorization**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design access control for an accounting app with client, accountant, support, and auditor roles.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Centralized policy improves consistency, while local enforcement keeps resource context available.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Add deny-by-default policies, tenant checks, audit logging, and security tests for horizontal privilege escalation.
keyPoints: Authentication is identity; authorization is permission.
Tokens require validation and lifecycle controls.
lessons.analogy: An office badge proves identity at the entrance, but room access still depends on the employee's role and the room's policy.
lessons.example: A SaaS backend verifies an OAuth access token, resolves tenant membership, applies role and resource policy, and records sensitive changes in an audit log.

lessons.title: Backend Design Challenge: Order Service
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A realistic backend combines contracts, transactions, asynchronous events, caching, rate controls, and recovery logic. An order service is useful because correctness matters while downstream systems remain unreliable.

## How it works

The create-order endpoint accepts an idempotency key, validates the cart, calculates price, creates an order in a pending state, and records an outbox event inside the same database transaction. Workers publish events for inventory reservation, payment, and notification. The order state machine makes pending, confirmed, cancelled, and failed transitions explicit. Reads use indexed queries and selective caching.

## Design decisions

- Keep the order database authoritative.
- Use an outbox so durable state and emitted events do not diverge.
- Model compensation when inventory or payment fails.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is charging payment synchronously before the order write commits. A timeout leaves the client uncertain and a retry may create another charge.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A relay race: each runner completes a defined leg and hands over a recorded baton; a failed leg triggers a recovery rule.

**Real-system connection:** Large commerce systems separate catalog browsing from correctness-sensitive checkout and coordinate downstream steps asynchronously.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **backend service design**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design order creation for a flash sale where payment and inventory services can time out.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Asynchronous coordination improves resilience but requires observable state and compensation.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use idempotency keys, local transactions, an outbox, DLQs, and workflow dashboards.

lessons.title: CAP Theorem
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

When network communication between nodes fails, a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee every request sees one consistent state and every request receives a successful response. CAP theorem forces designers to discuss behavior during partitions rather than promise vague perfection.

## How it works

Consistency in CAP means clients observe a single current value; availability means every request to a non-failing node receives a response; partition tolerance means the system continues operating despite lost or delayed messages between groups of nodes. Because real networks can partition, systems choose behavior per operation: reject or delay writes for stronger consistency, or accept writes and reconcile later for availability.

## Design decisions

- Discuss CAP only in the context of an actual partition.
- Different operations in one product may choose different behavior.
- Do not confuse CAP consistency with the full ACID transaction model.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is claiming a database is simply CP or AP without describing topology, operation, consistency level, or what the client experiences during a partition.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** Two branches of a bank lose connectivity. Should both approve withdrawals immediately, or should one pause risky actions until communication returns?

**Real-system connection:** A shopping site may keep browsing available from stale replicas while pausing inventory confirmation if it cannot safely prevent overselling.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **CAP theorem**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Choose partition behavior for product browsing, cart edits, and payment capture.
keyPoints: Consistency and availability can vary by operation.
Client-visible behavior matters more than labels.

lessons.title: Consistent Hashing
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Distributed caches and stores need to map keys to nodes. Simple modulo hashing works until the cluster size changes: many keys move at once, caches miss, and storage rebalancing becomes expensive.

## How it works

Consistent hashing places keys and nodes on a logical ring or uses a similar token scheme. Each key maps to a nearby node. Adding or removing a node moves only part of the keyspace. Virtual nodes or slots improve balance and make it easier to represent different capacities. Replicas protect data when a node disappears.

## Design decisions

- Balance workload, not only key count.
- Add virtual partitions so movement is controllable.
- Plan replication and hot-key mitigation separately.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is evenly distributing keys while one viral key receives most traffic. The cluster looks balanced by storage but one node remains overloaded.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A circular bus route assigns neighborhoods to the next depot on the route. Adding a depot changes only nearby assignments.

**Real-system connection:** Redis Cluster routes keys through hash slots, while Cassandra-style token partitioning distributes storage ownership across nodes.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **consistent hashing**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Explain what happens to cache hit ratio when a cluster adds one node.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Reduced remapping improves stability, while routing and rebalancing logic become more complex.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use virtual partitions, replicas, hotspot metrics, and key-splitting strategies.
keyPoints: Hot keys still need separate treatment.

lessons.title: Replication
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

One copy of data is a single point of failure. Replication stores copies on multiple nodes to improve read capacity, durability, regional locality, or recovery. The challenge is deciding how quickly copies must agree.

## How it works

Leader-follower replication sends writes to a primary and copies changes to replicas. Multi-leader and leaderless models trade simpler write ordering for different availability and conflict behavior. Synchronous replication waits for acknowledgements before success; asynchronous replication responds sooner but can lose recent updates or serve stale reads during failure.

## Design decisions

- Choose replication based on recovery objectives and consistency needs.
- Monitor replica lag as a user-impacting signal.
- Test promotion and failback rather than assuming they work.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is routing a user to an asynchronous replica immediately after a profile update. The response appears to lose the user's change even though replication catches up later.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A document has copies in several offices. Fast photocopying improves availability, but a newly edited version may not reach every office instantly.

**Real-system connection:** A read-heavy SaaS database keeps a primary for writes and replicas for reports while routing read-after-write flows to the primary.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **replication**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design profile reads after a user changes their display name.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Synchronous replication raises confidence but adds latency and may reduce write availability.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Measure lag, define read routing, automate guarded promotion, and rehearse recovery.
keyPoints: Lag affects freshness and failover safety.
Promotion is an operational procedure, not a magic switch.

lessons.example: A read-heavy SaaS database keeps a primary for writes and replicas for reports while routing read-after-write flows to the primary.

lessons.title: Distributed Transactions
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A business action often crosses services: reserve inventory, accept payment, create shipment, and notify a customer. A local database transaction cannot atomically control every remote dependency.

## How it works

Two-phase commit coordinates participants through prepare and commit phases, but can block and reduce availability. A saga instead records a workflow of local transactions and compensating actions. An outbox stores a business change and an event record in one local transaction so event publication can retry safely. Idempotency makes repeated work safe.

## Design decisions

- Prefer local transactions whenever possible.
- Use saga state to make progress and compensation observable.
- Treat exactly-once outcomes as a product of idempotency and deduplication, not wishful messaging guarantees.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is updating the order database and then publishing an event without an outbox. A crash between those steps creates an order that no downstream service learns about.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A travel itinerary books flight, hotel, and taxi separately. If the hotel fails, the system needs a defined cancellation or manual-review path.

**Real-system connection:** A checkout workflow writes an order and outbox event together, then coordinates inventory and payment through idempotent consumers.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **distributed transactions**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design a booking process when payment succeeds but reservation confirmation times out.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Availability and autonomy improve, while eventual consistency and workflow complexity increase.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Persist workflow state, add idempotency keys, monitor stuck steps, and define manual repair.
keyPoints: Compensation is not always identical to rollback.

lessons.title: CQRS and Event Sourcing
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Some domains need a clear audit history and read views shaped differently from write rules. CQRS separates command handling from query models; event sourcing persists changes as events rather than only storing the latest state.

## How it works

A command validates business rules and appends an immutable event. Projectors consume events and build read models for APIs, dashboards, or search. Snapshots reduce replay cost. Event schemas need versioning because past events are permanent contracts. CQRS can exist without event sourcing, and event sourcing can be excessive for ordinary CRUD.

## Design decisions

- Use these patterns only when domain and audit needs justify the cost.
- Make projections rebuildable.
- Version events for long-term compatibility.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is publishing low-level internal events that later become impossible to interpret or migrate. Every projection then depends on accidental implementation detail.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A bank statement records transactions and derives the current balance; it does not merely overwrite yesterday's balance.

**Real-system connection:** A financial ledger stores append-only entries and builds account summaries as projections for fast reads.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **CQRS and event sourcing**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Decide whether a project-management app really needs event sourcing.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Auditability and flexible reads improve, while storage, replay, and operational complexity increase.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Design versioned events, snapshots, idempotent projectors, and projection-lag monitoring.

Event history enables audit and rebuilds.
Schema evolution is a permanent responsibility.

lessons.example: A financial ledger stores append-only entries and builds account summaries as projections for fast reads.

lessons.title: Raft Consensus
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A replicated system needs a safe way to agree on ordered changes even when nodes fail or messages are delayed. Consensus algorithms solve agreement under defined fault assumptions.

## How it works

Raft elects a leader. The leader receives log entries, replicates them to followers, and commits an entry after a majority acknowledges it. Terms prevent stale leaders from acting indefinitely. Followers start elections when they stop hearing from a leader. A majority quorum means a five-node cluster can typically tolerate two unavailable nodes while still committing progress.

## Design decisions

- Consensus protects metadata and coordination, not unlimited application throughput.
- Odd-sized voting groups use resources efficiently.
- Avoid stretching a quorum across unreliable or high-latency links without understanding the effect.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is running only two voting nodes and expecting strong availability. Losing either node removes the majority required for safe progress.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A committee records decisions only after a majority signs the minutes; a former chair cannot continue approving changes after a new term begins.

**Real-system connection:** Kubernetes etcd and RabbitMQ quorum queues use consensus-based approaches for reliable replicated state.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **Raft consensus**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Explain why a three-node quorum cluster survives one failure but not two.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Safety improves, while cross-node coordination adds latency and limits write availability without quorum.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use three or five voting nodes, monitor elections, and test quorum loss behavior.
keyPoints: Leader election and quorum preserve safety.
Consensus is appropriate for small critical state, not every data path.

lessons.example: Kubernetes etcd and RabbitMQ quorum queues use consensus-based approaches for reliable replicated state.

lessons.title: Distributed Systems Design Challenge: Global Cart
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A global shopping cart appears simple but exposes consistency, latency, replication, and conflict questions. Users expect a fast cart across devices even when one region is impaired.

## How it works

Route a user to a nearby region, store cart items in a partitioned durable store, and identify mutations with idempotency keys and versions. Replicate cart state asynchronously across regions. Use deterministic merge rules for independent additions, and surface conflicts when automatic merging could surprise the customer. Inventory is not owned by the cart; validate and reserve it during checkout.

## Design decisions

- Separate cart convenience from checkout correctness.
- Design a version and conflict policy.
- Allow regional degradation without overselling inventory.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is decrementing authoritative inventory when an item enters a cart. Abandoned carts then lock stock and create a poor buying experience.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A shopping basket can hold a note saying 'I want this item,' but the warehouse reserves stock only at checkout.

**Real-system connection:** Large commerce systems keep browsing and cart interactions highly available while protecting payment and inventory confirmation with stricter workflows.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **distributed system design**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design cart behavior when a user edits from two devices during a regional network partition.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Local responsiveness improves, while conflicts and stale views need deliberate handling.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use idempotency keys, versioned writes, merge policy, region-aware routing, and checkout reservation.
keyPoints: Global UX may tolerate eventual cart consistency.
Conflict resolution is a product decision.

lessons.title: Cloud Providers and Shared Responsibility
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Cloud platforms offer building blocks for compute, storage, networking, identity, and managed data services. The value is speed and elasticity, not the elimination of architecture or security responsibilities.

## How it works

A region contains multiple isolated availability zones. Managed services reduce operational work, but the application owner still designs identity policies, data classification, backup, observability, quotas, and recovery. Infrastructure as code makes environments repeatable. Portability should be chosen deliberately: abstract the areas where switching matters, and accept provider-specific value where it improves delivery.

## Design decisions

- Design across failure domains rather than only across virtual machines.
- Understand the shared-responsibility boundary for every service.
- Use infrastructure as code and policy controls from the beginning.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is deploying all replicas and the database in one availability zone. The application appears redundant but fails when that zone is disrupted.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** Renting an apartment removes the need to build the structure, but the tenant still locks the door, protects belongings, and plans for emergencies.

**Real-system connection:** A production API can run across zones behind a load balancer while using a managed database with backups and tested failover.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **cloud provider architecture**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design a multi-zone API and database deployment for a business-critical SaaS application.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Provider-specific services improve productivity but can increase switching cost.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use multi-zone design, infrastructure as code, least privilege, quota review, and recovery tests.
keyPoints: Zones and regions are distinct failure domains.
Security and resilience remain application responsibilities.

lessons.example: A production API can run across zones behind a load balancer while using a managed database with backups and tested failover.

lessons.title: Serverless Architecture
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Many workloads have bursty traffic and spend long periods idle. Serverless platforms run code or workflows on demand while the provider handles provisioning and much of the scaling.

## How it works

Functions respond to HTTP requests, queue messages, object uploads, or schedules. Managed databases, queues, event buses, and object stores create a serverless architecture with minimal server administration. The application still needs limits: concurrency controls protect downstream databases, cold-start behavior affects latency, retries require idempotency, and execution-duration limits shape workload boundaries.

## Design decisions

- Choose functions for event-driven and bursty work.
- Protect downstream systems from sudden function concurrency.
- Keep deployment packages small and observable.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is connecting each rapidly scaling function directly to a relational database without pooling or a proxy. A small traffic spike exhausts database connections.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A taxi appears when requested instead of waiting outside every house all day, but a city still needs road capacity and dispatch rules.

**Real-system connection:** An upload pipeline stores a file in object storage, triggers a function to validate metadata, and enqueues heavier conversion work.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **serverless architecture**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design serverless invoice processing without overwhelming the database.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Operational simplicity improves, while platform constraints and usage-cost curves become important.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Apply reserved concurrency, DLQs, idempotency, tracing, and database-safe connection strategies.
keyPoints: Scale-out is not the same as unlimited downstream capacity.
lessons.analogy: A taxi appears when requested instead of waiting outside every house all day, but a city still needs road capacity and dispatch rules.
lessons.example: An upload pipeline stores a file in object storage, triggers a function to validate metadata, and enqueues heavier conversion work.

lessons.title: Containers and Kubernetes
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Teams need a repeatable way to package services and operate many instances reliably. Containers standardize runtime artifacts; Kubernetes coordinates scheduling, rollout, discovery, and recovery.

## How it works

A container image holds application code and dependencies. A Kubernetes Deployment manages desired replicas of Pods. Services provide stable discovery, readiness checks control traffic, and autoscalers adjust capacity. Resource requests help scheduling, while limits reduce noisy-neighbor risk. Kubernetes is a platform with operational cost; it should solve a real workload or organizational need.

## Design decisions

- Use immutable images and versioned releases.
- Treat Pods as disposable.
- Build platform defaults for health checks, logging, resource policies, and security.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is migrating a small application to Kubernetes before the team can operate the cluster. The resulting system is harder to debug than the original deployment.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** Shipping containers standardize cargo, while a port authority schedules cranes, routes containers, and tracks capacity.

**Real-system connection:** A platform team provides a supported deployment template so product teams can ship containerized services with consistent observability and policies.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **containers and Kubernetes**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design deployment defaults for a team shipping 30 containerized services.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Standardization and scale improve, while platform ownership and troubleshooting demands increase.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Provide golden paths, managed clusters, policy guardrails, and clear operational ownership.

Readiness, requests, and limits are production essentials.
Platform complexity must earn its keep.

lessons.title: CDN and Edge Architecture
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Global users experience network distance. Large files and repeated requests should not travel to a single origin every time. Edge architecture moves selected work and cached bytes closer to users.

## How it works

DNS directs users to edge locations. A CDN caches versioned static assets, media segments, and selected responses. Edge functions can normalize requests, redirect users, or apply lightweight policy. Origin shielding reduces duplicate origin fetches. Private content can use signed URLs or cookies. Cache keys, TTLs, and purge strategy determine correctness.

## Design decisions

- Cache immutable assets aggressively using versioned names.
- Keep edge logic lightweight and observable.
- Protect the origin from cache misses and attacks.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is including an authorization header in a cache key incorrectly or omitting user-specific dimensions. Private content may leak between users.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** Regional warehouses store popular products near customers, while specialized items still come from the central warehouse.

**Real-system connection:** Netflix Open Connect places playable content closer to viewers, while application APIs remain separate from the media-byte path.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **edge architecture**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Design CDN behavior for private training videos and public landing-page assets.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Latency and resilience improve, while cache invalidation and distributed debugging become harder.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Use versioned assets, signed access, origin shielding, TTL policy, and cache-hit monitoring.
keyPoints: Edge delivery reduces distance and origin load.
Cache policy is a correctness decision.

lessons.example: Netflix Open Connect places playable content closer to viewers, while application APIs remain separate from the media-byte path.

lessons.title: Multi-Region Architecture
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A regional outage, regulatory requirement, or global latency target may justify running a system in multiple regions. Multi-region is not a checkbox: data, routing, deployment, and operational control planes must be designed together.

## How it works

Active-passive architecture keeps a standby region for recovery. Active-active serves traffic from multiple regions and needs replication, conflict handling, and failover-safe routing. Stateless services are easier to duplicate than stateful databases. Recovery time objective defines how quickly service must return; recovery point objective defines acceptable data loss.

## Design decisions

- Choose active-passive unless business needs justify active-active complexity.
- Define data authority and conflict behavior.
- Test failover with dependencies, DNS, certificates, secrets, and operational tooling.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is replicating application servers but forgetting that the identity provider, configuration store, or deployment pipeline depends on the failed region.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A company opens a backup office, but it only helps if records, keys, phones, and decision authority are available there.

**Real-system connection:** A global SaaS product can serve reads locally while keeping selected correctness-sensitive writes in an authoritative region until active-active workflows are justified.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **multi-region architecture**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Choose active-passive or active-active for a payments dashboard and justify the choice.

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Resilience and locality improve, while replication, cost, and operational complexity rise.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Define RTO/RPO, dependency inventory, runbooks, failover drills, and data reconciliation.

lessons.title: Cloud Cost Optimization
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Cloud lets teams provision quickly, which also makes waste easy to create. Cost optimization is an architecture discipline: spend should follow user value, reliability requirements, and measured utilization.

## How it works

Break spend into compute, storage, network transfer, managed-service charges, licenses, and observability. Right-size instances, autoscale stateless capacity, use storage lifecycle policies, cache expensive transfer, and shut down unused environments. Unit economics such as cost per request, tenant, upload, or streamed hour make trends understandable. Reservations or commitments fit stable baselines; on-demand capacity fits uncertainty.

## Design decisions

- Measure cost by product unit, not only by monthly total.
- Optimize after finding the dominant spend category.
- Preserve reliability guardrails while reducing waste.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is reducing replica count or retention blindly to save money, then paying more through incidents and emergency scaling.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A household budget first identifies the largest recurring expenses rather than saving pennies while ignoring rent.

**Real-system connection:** A video platform can lower transfer and origin compute by serving popular segments from caches and applying lifecycle tiers to old source files.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **cloud cost optimization**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Reduce the monthly cost of an image-processing platform without harming user-visible reliability.

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Higher resilience and faster performance may cost more, but waste provides no user value.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Tag resources, track unit metrics, right-size, tier storage, and review data-transfer paths.

lessons.title: Case Study: Netflix on AWS and Open Connect
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

A global streaming platform demonstrates why one product can need both cloud compute and a specialized content-delivery network. Treating video delivery as ordinary API traffic would be inefficient.

## How it works

Control-plane services manage signup, browsing, playback authorization, recommendations, analytics, and operational workflows in cloud infrastructure. Playable video bytes follow a different path through Open Connect, Netflix's CDN program. Encoded media is placed close to viewers through ISP partnerships and interconnection. Clients can choose suitable bitrate and delivery source as network conditions change.

## Design decisions

- Separate control plane from data plane.
- Use edge-local delivery for large repeated content.
- Design clients to adapt when bandwidth or one delivery source degrades.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure in a simplified design is streaming every video segment from one cloud region. Origin transfer cost, network distance, and capacity demands become unnecessarily large.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A cinema chain stores popular films at local theaters while headquarters manages accounts, scheduling, and analytics.

**Real-system connection:** Netflix publicly describes Open Connect as a global network for efficiently delivering shows and movies closer to members.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. Design the first version of a video-learning platform and show how it could evolve at 100x scale.

lessons.title: OWASP Top 10 and Threat Modeling
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Security failures are usually system failures, not isolated bugs. Teams need a repeatable way to identify risks before attackers or incidents reveal them. OWASP's current released Top 10 is the 2025 edition, so training material should reflect the updated awareness baseline rather than freeze an older checklist.

## How it works

The OWASP Top 10:2025 highlights broken access control, security misconfiguration, software supply-chain failures, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, authentication failures, software or data integrity failures, security logging and alerting failures, and mishandling of exceptional conditions. Threat modeling adds application context: identify assets, entry points, trust boundaries, abuse cases, dependencies, failure paths, and mitigations for the actual product. The list is an awareness document, not a complete security standard.

## Design decisions

- Use the current OWASP Top 10 as a starting checklist, not a complete security program.
- Model authorization paths, tenant boundaries, dependencies, and exceptional conditions explicitly.
- Prioritize risks by business impact and realistic attack or failure path.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is scanning dependencies while ignoring insecure business logic. A fully patched endpoint can still let one customer read another customer's records, and a poorly handled dependency error can still leak data or bypass an important control.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A building inspection checks locks, wiring, emergency exits, visitor paths, and valuables rather than only testing one door.

**Real-system connection:** A document platform threat model covers upload validation, preview workers, share links, tenant access, audit logs, and SSRF protections for remote-import features.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **web application security**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Threat-model a feature that imports a document from a user-supplied URL.
keyPoints: Broken access control deserves special focus.
Current OWASP guidance includes supply-chain and exceptional-condition risks.

lessons.example: A document platform threat model covers upload validation, preview workers, share links, tenant access, audit logs, and SSRF protections for remote-import features.

lessons.title: JWT, OAuth, and SAML
lessons.theory:
## Why it matters

Identity systems are often implemented incorrectly because tokens, sessions, and delegated access are treated as interchangeable. A secure design starts with the actors and trust boundaries.

## How it works

OAuth 2.0 allows a client to obtain limited access to an HTTP service. OpenID Connect adds identity information for login use cases. JWT is a token format containing claims; it is not automatically an OAuth flow and should not be trusted without signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and algorithm validation. SAML uses signed XML assertions and remains common for enterprise single sign-on.

## Design decisions

- Use standards-based libraries and an identity provider.
- Keep access tokens short-lived and protect refresh tokens carefully.
- Validate intended audience and token type at every resource server.

## Failure mode to anticipate

A common failure is decoding a JWT and trusting its claims without verifying the signature and expected issuer. An attacker can forge identity or privileges.

## Practical lens

**Analogy:** A venue accepts official tickets only after checking issuer, event, date, and anti-counterfeit marks; merely reading printed text is insufficient.

**Real-system connection:** A SaaS product uses enterprise SSO, exchanges authorization through an identity provider, and enforces tenant permissions inside backend services.

A strong design does not stop at the diagram. Decide what should be measured, identify the first shared bottleneck, and describe the degraded behavior when one dependency becomes slow or unavailable. For **identity protocols**, the useful question is not “can this component be added?” but “which requirement does it satisfy, what new failure mode does it introduce, and how will the team know when the trade-off is no longer acceptable?”

## Apply it

Explain how a backend validates an access token before allowing invoice export.

## Senior-engineer check

Before implementation, write the assumption that would invalidate this design. Estimate peak load, define the consistency or freshness expectation, and choose one recovery test. The fastest architecture review is often a focused question: **Stateless validation improves scale, while revocation and lifecycle handling need explicit design.** Then verify the mitigation in a production-like environment: Validate tokens fully, rotate keys, protect refresh tokens, and log security-relevant events.
keyPoints: JWT is a format, not a complete security architecture.
SAML remains relevant for enterprise federation.
